entries.content_plain: Miscellaneous Maxims. 1 The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. See here, 1. What continual frights those are subject to that go on in wicked ways. Guilt in the conscience makes men a terror to themselves, so that they are ready to flee when none pursues; like one that absconds for debt, who thinks every one he meets a bailiff. Though they pretend to be easy, there are secret fears which haunt them wherever they go, so that they fear where no present or imminent danger is, Ps. liii. 5 . Those that have made God their enemy, and know it, cannot but see the whole creation at war with them, and therefore can have no true enjoyment of themselves, no confidence, no courage, but a fearful looking for of judgment. Sin makes men cowards. Degeneres animos timor arguit— Fear argues a degenerate soul. Virgil. Quos diri conscia facti mens habet attonitos— The consciousness of atrocious crimes astonishes and confounds. Juvenal . If they flee when none pursues, what will they do when they shall see God himself pursuing them with his armies? Job xx. 24 ; xv. 24 . See Deut. xxviii. 25 ; Lev. xxvi. 36 . 2. What a holy security and serenity of mind those enjoy who keep conscience void of offence and so keep themselves in the love of God: The righteous are bold as a lion, as a young lion; in the greatest dangers they have a God of almighty power to trust to. Therefore will not we fear though the earth be removed. Whatever difficulties they meet with in the way of their duty, they are not daunted by them. None of those things move me. Hic murus aheneus esto, nil conscire sibi— Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence, Still to preserve thy conscious innocence. Hor.

entries.content_osis: <l eID="gen14574" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14572"/> <div sID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A poor man that oppresseth the poor <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a sweeping rain which leaveth no food. <div eID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How hard-hearted poor people frequently are to one another, not only not doing such good offices as they might do one to another, but imposing upon and over-reaching one another. Those who know by experience the miseries of poverty should be compassionate to those who suffer the like, but they are inexcusably barbarous if they be injurious to them. 2. How imperious and griping those commonly are who, being indigent and necessitous, get into power. If a prince prefer a poor man, he forgets that ever he was poor, and none shall be so oppressive to the poor as he, nor squeeze them so cruelly. The hungry leech and the dry sponge suck most. <hi type="italic">Set a beggar on horseback, and he will ride</hi> without mercy. He <hi type="italic">is like a sweeping rain,</hi> which washes away the corn in the ground, and lays and beats out that which has grown, so that it <hi type="italic">leaves no food.</hi> Princes therefore ought not to put those into places of trust who are poor, and in debt, and behind-hand in the world, nor any who make it their main business to enrich themselves.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the law contend with them. <div eID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14578" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that <hi type="italic">praise the wicked</hi> make it to appear that they do themselves <hi type="italic">forsake the law,</hi> and go contrary to it, for that curses and condemns the wicked. Wicked people will speak well of one another, and so strengthen one another's hands in their wicked ways, hoping thereby to silence the clamours of their own consciences and to serve the interests of the devil's kingdom, which is not done by any thing so effectually as by keeping vice in reputation. 2. Those that do indeed make conscience of the law of God themselves will, in their places, vigorously oppose sin, and bear their testimony against it, and do what they can to shame and suppress it. They will reprove the works of darkness, and silence the excuses which are made for those works, and do what they can to bring gross offenders to punishment, that others may hear and fear.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse <hi type="italic">in his</hi> ways, though he <hi type="italic">be</hi> rich. <div eID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is supposed that a man may <hi type="italic">walk in his uprightness</hi> and yet be poor in this world, which is a temptation to dishonesty, and yet may resist the temptation and continue to <hi type="italic">walk in his uprightness</hi>—also that a man may be <hi type="italic">perverse in his ways,</hi> injurious to God and man, and yet be rich, and prosper in the world, for a while, may be rich, and so lie under great obligations and have great opportunities to do good, and yet be <hi type="italic">perverse in his ways</hi> and do a great deal of hurt. 2. It is maintained as a paradox to a blind world that an honest, godly, poor man, is better than a wicked, ungodly, rich man, has a better character, is in a better condition, has more comfort in himself, is a greater blessing to the world, and is worthy of much more honour and respect. It is not only certain that his case will be better at death, but it is better in life. When Aristides was by a rich man upbraided with his poverty he answered, <hi type="italic">Thy riches do thee more hurt than my poverty does me.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Whoso keepeth the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wise son: but he that is a companion of riotous <hi type="italic">men</hi> shameth his father. <div eID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14585" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Religion is true wisdom, and it makes men wise in every relation. He that conscientiously <hi type="italic">keeps the law</hi> is wise, and he will be particularly <hi type="italic">a wise son,</hi> that is, will act discreetly towards his parents, for the law of God teaches him to do so. 2. Bad company is a great hindrance to religion. Those that are <hi type="italic">companions of riotous men,</hi> that choose such for their companions and delight in their conversation, will certainly be drawn from <hi type="italic">keeping the law of God</hi> and drawn to transgress it, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>. 3. Wickedness is not only a reproach to the sinner himself, but to all that are akin to him. He that keeps rakish company, and spends his time and money with them, not only grieves his parents, but shames them; it turns to their disrepute, as if they had not done their duty to him. They are ashamed that a child of theirs should be scandalous and abusive to their neighbours.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue. <div eID="gen14616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14617" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Flatterers may please those for a time who, upon second thoughts, will detest and despise them. If ever they come to be convinced of the evil of those sinful courses they were flattered in, and to be ashamed of the pride and vanity which were humoured and gratified by those flatteries, they will hate the fawning flatterers as having had an ill design upon them, and the fulsome flatteries as having had an ill effect upon them and become nauseous. 2. Reprovers may displease those at first who yet afterwards, when the passion is over and the bitter physic begins to work well, will love and respect them. He that cries out against his surgeon for hurting him when he is searching his wound will yet pay him well, and thank him too, when he has cured it.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack: but he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse. <div eID="gen14624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A promise to the charitable: <hi type="italic">He that gives to the poor</hi> shall himself be never the poorer for so doing; he <hi type="italic">shall not lack.</hi> If he have but little, and so be in danger of lacking, let him give out of his little, and that will prevent it from coming to nothing; as the bounty of the widow of Sarepta to Elijah (for whom she made a little cake first) saved what she had, when it was reduced to a handful of meal. If he have much, let him give much out of it, and that will prevent its growing less; he and his shall not want what is given in pious charity. What we gave we have. 2. Woeful is the condition of that man who has the word of God and the prayers of the poor against him.
